properties.name: The schema DOES bound decomposition downward — `component` is a hard floor and there is no `assembly` rung — correcting this requirement's own 2026-08-07 line that 'the schema does not bound this; the population does'
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-25, by hitting it. Modelling the two `KvBackend` implementations as parts of `cmp:byte-store` — where they physically live, in one file — produced:

    hierarchy_issues -> 2 x level_mismatch
    'cmp:byte-store' (component) contains 'cmp:memory-backend' (component)
     but a parent must be above its child

🛑 THIS CORRECTS A LINE IN THIS REQUIREMENT'S OWN MEASUREMENT. Its 2026-08-07 text reads: *"DEPTH IS TWO, not 'as deep as the design needs'. ... nothing above system-of-systems and nothing below component. **The schema does not bound this; the population does.**"* The second half is TRUE UPWARD and FALSE DOWNWARD. `schema/structure.yaml:18` declares `level` as a closed enum — `[component, subsystem, system, system_of_systems, enterprise]` — and `component` is rank 0 in `hierarchy.rs::Level::rank()`. **There is no value to give a part of a component, so the containment cannot be expressed at all**, and promoting the parent to `subsystem` only moves the mismatch up into `sys:foundation`. The population is not what stopped it here; the vocabulary did.

⚠️ AND THE LADDER IS DECLARED TWICE, WHICH IS THE HAZARD ANY FIX MUST NOT INHERIT. `schema/structure.yaml` holds the enum; `crates/reflow2-core/src/hierarchy.rs` holds `Level` with `as_str`, `from_key` and `rank`. Nothing checks they agree, and `from_key` maps ANY unrecognised string to `Component` — so a rung added to the YAML and forgotten in Rust silently ranks 0 and every containment involving it reads as a mismatch. That is a silent fallback in a project holding `req:no-silent-fallback` at critical priority, and it is the same two-places-one-truth shape the absorption found in `#[non_exhaustive]` match arms.

⭐⭐ ANTHONY'S RESEARCH, 2026-08-25, WHICH NAMES THE MISSING RUNG AND WHY A FIXED LADDER CANNOT WORK. The canonical SE hierarchy is four tiers, and reflow2 is missing the third:

    tier          aerospace example          software example
    System        commercial airliner        e-commerce platform
    Subsystem     avionics / flight control  payment processing
    ASSEMBLY      autopilot computer         microservice / API gateway     <- ABSENT
    Component     microprocessor chip (LRU)  single code module / class

⭐ THE DECISIVE POINT IS NOT THE MISSING RUNG, IT IS THAT **"ATOMIC" SHIFTS BY DOMAIN.** In his table the atomic unit is a microprocessor chip for aerospace and a code module for software. A ladder with fixed named rungs asserts that every domain bottoms out at the same conceptual depth, and his examples show they do not. That is the argument for an OPEN ladder rather than one more enum value.

HIS FOUR STOPPING RULES, recorded as reference because they are the answer to "how deep is deep enough" and nothing in reflow2 says it:
1. **BLACK BOX PROCUREMENT** — if you buy it from a vendor as a complete unit, stop. An airliner's engine is atomic to the airframer; you do not decompose the turbine.
2. **MAINTENANCE / LRU** — stop where a technician pulls one part out and puts a new one in. A DIMM is an LRU; the transistors on it are not.
3. **SINGLE DISCIPLINE / SINGLE OWNER** — stop when a box can be handed to one discipline or one small team. A braking subsystem is cross-disciplinary; a bracket is pure mechanical, a driver module pure software.
4. **VERIFICATION COST** — every decomposition creates an item that must be tested, documented and tracked. Stop when verifying the parts costs more than the risk of testing them together.

📌 RULE 1 IS ALREADY A KNOWN GAP HERE, and this is where it lands: `anthony-thinks-about-over-engineering` records that **nothing in reflow2 distinguishes a component that was BOUGHT from one that was BUILT**. That distinction is exactly what rule 1 turns on — a bought box is atomic by procurement, whatever its internal complexity.

📌 BOUNDS: measured on one containment attempt in one design. The upward half of the ladder was not re-tested and the requirement's claim about it stands. No fix is proposed here — whether the answer is one more enum value (`assembly`) or an open user-defined ladder is a live question, and the second is what Anthony asked for in his own words: *"should be allowed to go as many rungs down as the user needs."*
